notes.meaning: David pronounces a blessing on the person who truly cares for the poor. "Poor" here means anyone weak or low: short of money, sick, looked down on, or downhearted. To "care for" them means more than tossing them a coin. It means looking into their trouble, helping wisely, and judging them kindly instead of assuming their suffering proves God is angry with them. God promises to show mercy to such a person when his own day of trouble comes.

differ.view: The psalm is mainly David's own experience. Jesus later applied verse 9 to Judas, and Christ is the highest example of one who cared for the poor.
The whole psalm speaks of Christ. He is the "poor one" of this verse, and the enemies are those who wanted Him dead.

notes.meaning: God will guard the merciful person, keep him alive, and bless him in this life. He will not hand him over to what his enemies want. The promise is not that he will be made great, but that he will be kept safe. If earthly gains do not come, spiritual blessings will. The last line can also be read as a prayer: "Do not give him up to his enemies."

When this person lies sick, God will hold him up. Some read the second line as God tenderly remaking the sick bed, like a nurse or a mother, so the person is comforted while ill. Others read it as God turning the sickbed into health. Matthew Henry adds that God has not promised His people they will never be sick or die. He has promised to give them strength and peace to bear it.

Now David turns to his own prayer. He does not ask for what he has earned. He throws himself on God's mercy and openly admits, "I have sinned against You." Sin is a sickness of the soul. God's forgiveness and renewing grace heal it, and we should want that healing even more than bodily health. Strangely, David's confession is itself his plea: he has no claim, so he leans on God's free kindness.

David's enemies speak cruelly about him while he is sick. They wish he would die and that even his memory would vanish. Wishing a sick man dead is about as cruel as it gets. Yet his name did not perish. It lives on in Scripture.

One man comes to visit as if he were a caring friend. But his kind words are false. All the while, his heart is collecting anything he can twist against David. As soon as he leaves the room, he spreads it around as gossip.

Everyone who hates David passes the visitor's report along in whispers and imagines the worst. They say some terrible, deadly thing has been poured out on him and stuck fast, and he will never get up again. They took his illness as a sign that God had turned against him for good. The phrase may refer to the disease itself or to a shameful charge stuck to his name.

Worst of all, even David's close friend, "the man of my peace," turned on him. This was someone he trusted and who ate at his table. "Lifting up the heel" pictures a horse kicking the master who feeds it. Many think David meant Ahithophel, his trusted adviser who joined Absalom's rebellion. Jesus applied this verse to Judas, who ate with Him and then betrayed Him (John 13:18).

differ.view: The words were true of David, but the Holy Spirit was also looking ahead and speaking of Christ and Judas.
The verse is not a direct prediction. David's betrayal is a pattern that Jesus' betrayal by Judas fulfilled in a fuller way.

notes.meaning: David turns from cruel people to God: "But You, O LORD, be gracious to me." He asks God to raise him from his sickbed. "That I may repay them" is understood as a king's duty to bring lawful justice on traitors, not private revenge. Some also read it as a wish to repay evil with good. Spurgeon notes the gospel calls us to a gentler spirit.

David takes it as a sign of God's love and delight in him that his enemy has not won. They hoped he would die, but God kept him. We should not enjoy our enemies' downfall. But we may be glad when their evil plans fail. Seeing God's favour in a mercy makes that mercy doubly sweet.

David's integrity, meaning his honest and upright heart, lasts only because God holds him up. Left to ourselves we would fall. God keeps him in His presence, under His caring eye, forever. That points to the joy of being with God for all time.

The psalm ends in praise to the LORD, the God of Israel. That is His title as the God who made a covenant, a binding promise, with His people. He is praised from everlasting to everlasting, with no beginning and no end. The double "Amen" means "So be it!" and shows heartfelt joy. This verse also closes the first of the five books of Psalms.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: This blessing may not be part of the original psalm. It may have been added by whoever collected the first book of Psalms, as its closing line.
